sections.title: Coding in the terminal
sections.why: No IDE needed. Editor + compiler + runner, all text. Same pattern for every language: write → compile/build → run.

callouts.title: why ./hello and not just hello?
callouts.body: The shell only searches the folders in your `PATH` (system bin folders) — for safety, your current folder is not in it. `./` says “the program right here”.

callouts.title: terminal editor as your C IDE
callouts.body: Write in `vim` or `nano`, compile with `gcc`, split the screen with `tmux` (`sudo dnf install tmux`) to see code and output side by side. That's the whole “IDE”.

rows: all warnings on — meets the bugs before they bite
debug info, lets gdb show line numbers

preBlocks: # 1. write the code nano hello.c # 2. compile: source file -> executable named "hello" gcc hello.c -o hello # 3. run it. The ./ is required (see below) ./hello
# Makefile — note: tabs, not spaces, before gcc app: main.c utils.c gcc -Wall main.c utils.c -o app # then just: make ./app

sections.title: Services & logs
sections.why: Modern Linux is run by systemd. Two tools run the show: `systemctl` controls services, `journalctl` reads their logs.

callouts.title: the distinction that prevents disasters
callouts.body: `systemctl` = system-wide services (network, display manager). `systemctl --user` = your session's services (KDE, apps). Desktop problems are usually user services — no sudo.

rows: is it running? recent errors? (no sudo needed)
previous boot — golden after a crash/forced shutdown

sections.title: Clock & time
sections.why: A wrong clock breaks logins, TLS certificates and tokens while your timezone looks perfectly fine. One command diagnoses it.

commands.description: Everything at once: system clock, RTC (motherboard clock), timezone, NTP state.

rows.value: Everything at once: system clock, RTC (motherboard clock), timezone, NTP state.

callouts.title: gotcha
callouts.body: `NTP service: active` only means the sync daemon runs — not that it succeeded. The line that matters is `System clock synchronized: yes`.

sections.title: When the GUI dies
sections.why: Black screen, dropped to a TTY (full-screen text login)? Don't reboot yet — the system is fine, the graphical layer just fell over.

commands.description: Switches between virtual terminals. Your GUI sits on one TTY; F3 gives you a spare one to work from.

rows.value: Switches between virtual terminals. Your GUI sits on one TTY; F3 gives you a spare one to work from.

sections.title: Snap apps & KWallet
sections.why: Snap apps are sandboxed, so they ask KDE's KWallet for secrets — and KWallet asks you for its password. Repeatedly.

callouts.title: diagnose the layer, not the app
callouts.body: The chain is `app → D-Bus → your session's credential service → KWallet → unlock prompt`. The prompt proves the chain reached KWallet — not that the app or Snap is broken.

callouts.title: no sudo here, ever
callouts.body: KWallet and KDE session services belong to your user. `sudo`-ing them breaks things and fixes nothing.

sections.title: Black screen after suspend
sections.why: Suspend involves the kernel, GPU driver, firmware and the desktop. A machine can resume at kernel level while the screen stays black — so read the log before changing anything.

callouts.title: gotchas that waste afternoons
callouts.body: NVIDIA fixes don't apply if Intel drives your screen (check which GPU owns the display first). ACPI errors near suspend = firmware talking, not necessarily the cause. Don't touch GRUB or kernel parameters before the log names the guilty subsystem.

sections.title: NTFS cleanup & disks
sections.why: Cleaning a Windows partition from Fedora, safely: look → identify → verify → delete the exact target → verify.

commands.description: Look first, delete the exact directory second, verify with `ls`/`du` third.

rows.value: Look first, delete the exact directory second, verify with `ls`/`du` third.

sections.title: Danger zone
sections.why: Commands that can wreck a system in one keystroke. Know them to avoid them — not to use them.

callouts.title: sudo rm -rf /
callouts.body: `rm -rf` is irreversible: no trash, no undo, no “are you sure”. A typo in the path has destroyed systems. Mitigation: type the path, Tab-complete it, `ls` it first — only then prefix with `rm -rf`.

callouts.title: dd if=... of=/dev/sdX
callouts.body: Writes raw bytes straight to a disk, bypassing every safeguard. One wrong letter in `of=` = wiped drive. Triple-check with `lsblk` before even thinking about it.

callouts.title: curl ... | bash
callouts.body: Runs whatever a website hands you, as you. Read the script first, or at least know the source.

callouts.title: the mindset that keeps systems alive
callouts.body: Diagnose the layer before changing it → change one thing → verify → repeat. Read-only commands first (`status`, `ls`, `journalctl`), mutating commands last. sudo is the last resort, not the first tool.
